title: Global connections and the structure of skills in local co-worker networks
abstract: Social connections that reach distant places are advantageous for individuals, firms and cities, providing access to new skills and knowledge. However, systematic evidence on how firms build global knowledge access is still lacking. In this paper, we analyse how global work connections relate to differences in the skill composition of employees within companies and local industry clusters. We gather survey data from 10% of workers in a local industry in Sweden, and complement this with digital trace data to map co-worker networks and skill composition.
summary_en: Companies and cities that connect to distant places benefit from inflows of new ideas — but how exactly are these global connections built? Lőrincz and co-authors combine survey responses from 10% of workers in a Swedish industrial cluster with digital-trace data on co-worker networks and find that firms with more international ties also employ a measurably wider range of skills. Globally connected firms aren't just better at importing knowledge: their internal skill mix is richer, in a way that is observable in network and trace data, not just in stated international activity.
data_used: Survey of ~10% of workers in a single Swedish local industry cluster, combined with digital-trace data (LinkedIn-style employment histories) on co-worker networks. Skill composition extracted from worker profiles; network metrics derived from co-employment histories.
policy_relevance: For Hungarian regional and innovation policy (HIPA's FDI playbook, county-level smart-specialisation strategies): supports the case for actively cultivating outbound research and worker mobility links to global hubs as a tool for diversifying the local skill base, not just for marketing exports. Caveat: based on a single Swedish cluster, so the magnitudes don't translate directly to, say, Debrecen or Győr.
